noteBlocks.lede: A pulse sent out and caught again tells you how far away something is. Ships find the seabed that way, hospitals find a baby, engineers find cracks inside steel. There is one number in it that has to be handled carefully.

noteBlocks.caption: One pulse, two journeys: the timer runs from the moment the pulse leaves until its echo is back.

noteBlocks.md: A pulse that comes back has made **two journeys**: out to whatever reflected it, and back again. The timer starts when the pulse leaves and stops when the echo arrives, so the time you are given always covers **both journeys**.

noteBlocks.title: Why every echo has a factor of two
noteBlocks.md: The pulse travels at one steady speed, down through the water and back up through the same water. So the two journeys take equal times, and each takes half of the measured time. Half the time means half the distance: every factor of two in this topic comes from that.

noteBlocks.stem: A ship's echo sounder records 0.14 s between sending a pulse and receiving its echo from the seabed. How long did the pulse take to reach the seabed? [1]

steps.working: The timer ran from pulse to echo: 0.14 s.
steps.decision: Say first what the measured time covers: from the pulse leaving the ship to the echo arriving back.

steps.working: In that time the pulse went down to the seabed and came back up: two equal journeys.
steps.decision: The speed is the same on the way down and on the way up, so the two journeys take the same time.

steps.working: Time to reach the seabed = 0.14 ÷ 2 = 0.07 s
steps.decision: One journey is half of the there-and-back time.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ship sends a sonar pulse straight down and times the echo. In the time its timer measures, how far does the pulse travel?
options: down to the seabed and back up again
down to the seabed only
half of the way down to the seabed
noteBlocks.answer: down to the seabed and back up again
noteBlocks.explain: The timer starts as the pulse leaves the ship and stops when the echo is back, so it covers the trip down and the trip back up, as step 2 of the See it shows. The answer: down to the seabed and back up again. Down to the seabed only is the depth, half of the path the timer covers.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the depth is what you want, but the timer keeps running until the echo is back at the ship, so it also times the trip up.

optionNotes.option: half of the way down to the seabed
optionNotes.why: Halving is done to the distance after the calculation; the timer itself runs for the whole path, down and back.

twin.prompt: A bat calls and times the echo from a cave wall. In the time the bat measures, how far does its call travel?
options: to the wall and back again
to the wall only
half of the way to the wall
twin.answer: to the wall and back again
twin.explain: The bat's timing runs from its call to the echo, so the call goes out to the wall and returns. The answer: to the wall and back again. To the wall only is the one-way distance, half of the path.

optionNotes.why: The bat's timer keeps running until the echo is back, so the call covers the return trip too; the wall is only halfway along its path.

optionNotes.option: half of the way to the wall
optionNotes.why: Halving comes after the calculation, to turn the path into a distance; the call itself travels the whole path, out and back.

noteBlocks.text: 2. From an echo time to a distance

noteBlocks.md: Use the speed equation you already know, v = d/t, turned round to d = v × t. With the whole measured time in it, v × t gives the **total** path, there and back. The distance to the reflector is **half** of that total.

noteBlocks.title: The echo rule
noteBlocks.md: **distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2**. No physics equation is printed on the paper. The first mark is for a correct equation, so v = d/t written first earns it; the substitution, the total distance and the halved answer then earn a mark each.

noteBlocks.stem: A climber claps at the mouth of a cave and hears the echo from the back wall 1.2 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate the distance to the back wall. [4]

steps.working: v = d/t, so d = v × t
steps.decision: Write the equation before any number. It earns the first mark, and a wrong equation scores nothing.
Put in the speed and the whole measured time.
This is the total path: the sound reached the wall and returned.
Halve it: the wall is one journey away. The answer must be smaller than the total.

noteBlocks.prompt: A diver's sonar pulse returns from a wreck 0.024 s after it was sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. How far away is the wreck, in m?
noteBlocks.explain: Speed × time gives the whole path out and back: 1500 × 0.024 = 36 m, as in step 3 of the See it. The wreck is one journey away, half of that: 18 m. If you wrote 36, that is the there-and-back total; halve it once.

twin.prompt: A shout echoes from a wall 0.7 s after it is made. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the wall, in m?
twin.explain: 340 × 0.7 = 238 m is the path there and back, so the wall is 238 ÷ 2 = 119 m away.

noteBlocks.text: 3. From a known distance to a speed

noteBlocks.md: Sometimes the paper gives the distance and asks for the speed. The factor of two now runs the other way: in the measured time the wave covered the distance **twice**, so **double the distance** before you divide by the time. Halving the time instead gives the same answer, and either route earns the marks.

noteBlocks.stem: A student stands 99 m from a tall wall and claps once. The echo returns 0.6 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in the air. [4]

steps.decision: The equation first, as always.
The clap went to the wall and back, so the sound covered the 99 m twice.
Divide by the whole measured time: it matches the whole path.
The answer with its unit. Halving the time instead, 99 ÷ 0.3, gives the same 330 m/s.

noteBlocks.prompt: A clap echoes back from a wall 34 m away, 0.2 s later. What is the speed of sound, in m/s?
noteBlocks.explain: The sound covered 2 × 34 = 68 m in 0.2 s, as step 2 of the See it doubles the distance, so v = 68 ÷ 0.2 = 340 m/s. If you wrote 170, that divided the one-way 34 m by the there-and-back time; double the distance first.

twin.prompt: A sonar pulse returns from the seabed 45 m below a ship 0.06 s after it was sent. What is the speed of sound in the water, in m/s?
twin.explain: The pulse covered 2 × 45 = 90 m in 0.06 s, so the speed is 90 ÷ 0.06 = 1500 m/s.

noteBlocks.caption: Above 20 000 Hz a human ear hears nothing, but it is still sound: that is ultrasound.

noteBlocks.md: **Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency greater than **20 000 Hz**, too high for a human ear. It is still sound, so it is **longitudinal** and needs particles to travel through. Keep it apart from **ultraviolet**, which is electromagnetic: the two words have been swapped in tables on more than one paper.

noteBlocks.stem: An ultrasonic pest repeller gives out sound of frequency 28 kHz. Explain whether this sound is ultrasound. [2]

steps.decision: Kilo means a thousand: turn the frequency into hertz before you compare it.
Compare it with the threshold, the one number the definition carries.

steps.working: So it is ultrasound: sound too high for a human to hear.
steps.decision: Finish with the conclusion in the question's own words.

noteBlocks.prompt: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency greater than ______ Hz.
noteBlocks.explain: The threshold is the top of human hearing, 20 000 Hz, the number the pest repeller's 28 000 Hz was compared with in step 2 of the See it. The number is what earns the mark: very high-pitched on its own does not.

twin.prompt: Written in kilohertz, the lowest frequency of ultrasound is ______ kHz.
twin.explain: 20 000 Hz is 20 kHz, because one kilohertz is 1000 hertz.

noteBlocks.md: The specification names two uses of ultrasound. In **industry** it finds **defects in metals**; in **medicine** it measures the **head diameter of a foetus**. Both work the same way. A pulse reflects from **every boundary** it meets, so one pulse sends back several echoes. An **earlier echo means a nearer boundary**, and each time becomes a depth with the same halving.

noteBlocks.caption: A real scan. Every bright line in it is an echo, placed on the screen by the time it took to come back.
noteBlocks.prompt: The sonographer puts two markers on the screen and the machine prints a length in millimetres. Explain how a machine that only measures times can print a length, and say what else it has to be told before it can.

noteBlocks.stem: An ultrasound pulse is sent into a metal block. One echo returns after 0.00004 s and a second after 0.00012 s. Ultrasound travels at 5000 m/s in this metal. Find the depth of the crack and the thickness of the block. [4]

steps.working: First echo: 5000 × 0.00004 = 0.2 m there and back
steps.decision: The earlier echo comes from the nearer boundary, the crack.
Halve it, as for any echo.

steps.working: Second echo: 5000 × 0.00012 = 0.6 m there and back
steps.decision: The later echo comes from the far face of the block.
Halve again. The crack lies 0.1 m down inside a block 0.3 m thick.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Physics Revision "Ultrasound"
noteBlocks.why: Freesciencelessons on what ultrasound is and how an echo time becomes a distance, beside our own worked steps.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two echoes come back from one pulse sent into a steel block. What does the earlier one tell the engineer?
options: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
the block is made of two different metals
the pulse is travelling faster near the surface
noteBlocks.answer: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
noteBlocks.explain: An earlier echo has had a shorter journey, because the speed is the same all through the block: in the See it the first echo came back from the crack, only 0.1 m down. So the earlier echo means something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface. No second metal or change of speed is needed.

optionNotes.option: the block is made of two different metals
optionNotes.why: A join between two metals would reflect too, but nothing in the reading says there is one; an earlier echo simply came from something nearer, such as a crack.

optionNotes.option: the pulse is travelling faster near the surface
optionNotes.why: A shorter time could come from a higher speed, but the speed is the same all through one block, so only a shorter journey explains the earlier echo.

twin.prompt: A scanner sends one ultrasound pulse into a patient and receives two echoes. Which echo came from the boundary nearer the probe?
options: the echo that arrived first
the echo that arrived last
the louder of the two echoes
twin.explain: Both echoes travel at the same speed, so the one with the shorter journey arrives first. The answer: the echo that arrived first. Loudness does not tell you the distance.

optionNotes.why: The later echo had further to go: at one speed a longer journey takes longer, so it came from the boundary further from the probe.

optionNotes.option: the louder of the two echoes
optionNotes.why: Loudness depends on how much of the pulse a boundary reflects, not on how far away it is; the arrival time gives the distance.

noteBlocks.md: **Sonar** sends **pulses of sound** through water, to find the seabed, a shoal of fish or a wreck. **Radar** sends pulses of **electromagnetic waves**, radio waves or microwaves, through the air, to find **aircraft and ships**. Radar pulses travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so an echo from an aircraft tens of kilometres away is back in less than a thousandth of a second.

noteBlocks.stem: (a) A trawler must find a shoal of fish under the water. Say whether it should use sonar or radar, and give a reason. [2] (b) An airport's radar echo from an aircraft returns 0.00012 s after the pulse is sent. Radio waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the distance to the aircraft in km. [4]

steps.working: (a) Sonar: the shoal is under water, and sonar sends pulses of sound through water.
steps.decision: Under water it is sonar, and sonar is sound; radar is for aircraft and ships.
Radar is electromagnetic, so its pulse travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
On a calculator, type 3 × 10⁸ as 3E8. This is the path out to the aircraft and back.

steps.working: Distance to the aircraft = 36 000 ÷ 2 = 18 000 m = 18 km
steps.decision: Halve for one journey, then divide by 1000 for kilometres.

noteBlocks.prompt: A lifeboat crew must find a sunken boat on the seabed and also track a helicopter above the sea. Which pairing is right?
options: seabed: sonar, sending sound pulses; helicopter: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
seabed: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: sonar, sending sound pulses
seabed: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: radar, sending sound pulses
noteBlocks.answer: seabed: sonar, sending sound pulses; helicopter: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
noteBlocks.explain: Under water the system is sonar, and sonar sends sound (step 1 of the See it); through the air to an aircraft it is radar, which sends electromagnetic waves (step 2). So the seabed takes sonar with sound pulses and the helicopter radar with electromagnetic waves. Swapping either the systems or the waves loses the mark.

optionNotes.option: seabed: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: sonar, sending sound pulses
optionNotes.why: This swaps the two systems: radar is for aircraft and ships, and sonar is for objects under the water.

optionNotes.option: seabed: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: radar, sending sound pulses
optionNotes.why: The systems are right but the waves are swapped: sonar sends pulses of sound, and radar sends electromagnetic waves.

twin.prompt: A harbour tracks a ship arriving on the surface while divers map a wreck below it. Which pairing is right?
options: ship: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; wreck: sonar, sending sound pulses
ship: sonar, sending sound pulses; wreck: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
ship: radar, sending sound pulses; wreck: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves
twin.answer: ship: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; wreck: sonar, sending sound pulses
twin.explain: Ships and aircraft are found by radar, which sends electromagnetic waves; anything under water is found by sonar, which sends sound. So the ship takes radar and the wreck sonar.

optionNotes.option: ship: sonar, sending sound pulses; wreck: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
optionNotes.why: This swaps the two systems: radar finds ships and aircraft above the water, and sonar finds things beneath it.

optionNotes.option: ship: radar, sending sound pulses; wreck: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves
optionNotes.why: The systems are right, but the waves are swapped: radar sends electromagnetic waves and sonar sends pulses of sound.

noteBlocks.md: **Distance given, speed wanted.** The stem gives the distance to a wall and the time to the wall and back, then asks for the speed (Summer 2024 Higher). Double the distance, or halve the time, before you divide.

**A frequency in kilohertz.** The wave equation turns up inside an ultrasound question with the frequency in kHz (Summer 2025 Higher) or in standard form (Summer 2024 Higher). Change it to hertz first: that conversion earns a mark of its own.

**Ultrasound or ultraviolet?** A table of waves to sort (Summer 2023 and 2025 Foundation) is lost on one word. Ultrasound is sound, so it goes with the longitudinal waves. Ultraviolet is electromagnetic, so it goes with the transverse waves.

noteBlocks.stem: A bat's call has a frequency of 68 kHz and travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate its wavelength. [4]

steps.decision: The wave equation. Recall it: the paper does not print it.
Convert before you substitute: kilo is a thousand, and the conversion earns its own mark.
Substitute the speed and the frequency in hertz.
Rearrange and finish with the unit: 5 mm, sensibly short for ultrasound.

noteBlocks.prompt: An ultrasound probe works at 25 kHz in water, where sound travels at 1500 m/s. What is the wavelength, in m?
noteBlocks.explain: Convert first: 25 kHz is 25 000 Hz, as in step 2 of the See it. Then λ = v ÷ f = 1500 ÷ 25 000 = 0.06 m. If you wrote 60, the kilo was left out, which makes the wavelength a thousand times too long.

twin.prompt: A parking sensor on a car sends ultrasound of frequency 55 kHz through air, where sound travels at 330 m/s. What is the wavelength, in m?

Speed times time always gives the distance the wave actually covered — and the timer ran for the whole journey.
Halve it, because that total is the trip down plus the trip back up.

options: Because the pulse travelled down to the seabed and back up to the ship
Because the echo is half as loud as the pulse
Because sound travels half as fast on the way back

Calculate the speed of sound in the water. [3]

steps.decision: Going the other way round, the factor of two is a doubling, not a halving: the pulse covered the depth twice.

options: Because the 0.08 s covers the journey down and the journey back up
Because the speed of sound doubles in water
Because two echoes were received
whyMenu.explain: The time you are given is always the there-and-back time. When you want a distance you halve; when you want a speed you double the one-way distance first.

steps.decision: Now an ordinary speed calculation, with the corrected distance in it.
Finish with the unit. Sound in sea water is around 1500 m/s, so this is believable.

twin.stem:
A clap is echoed from a wall 68 m away, 0.4 s after it was made.
Calculate the speed of sound in the air. [3]

items.stem: Before we start, from P1: rearranged to give a distance, what does speed = distance ÷ time become?

options.feedback: That rearrangement is the engine of every echo calculation.
Dividing by the time would make a long journey come out short. Multiply.
That is upside down. Distance = speed × time.

items.stem: From the last topic: sound is which kind of wave?

options.feedback: Longitudinal, and so is ultrasound, which is only sound too high to hear.
Water waves and electromagnetic waves are transverse. Sound is longitudinal — the waves topic covers this first.

items.stem: How many milliseconds are there in one second?

options.feedback: 1000. Echo times often arrive in milliseconds and have to be converted before substituting.
Milli means a thousandth, so there are 1000 milliseconds in a second.
60 is seconds in a minute. Milli means a thousandth.

options.text: sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz
options.feedback: That is the specification's wording, and the number is what carries the mark.
Those are two different things. Ultraviolet is electromagnetic; ultrasound is sound. Examiners have reported the two words being swapped.

options.text: a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum
options.feedback: Ultrasound is sound, so it is longitudinal and it needs particles to travel through. Only electromagnetic waves cross a vacuum.

items.stem: A sonar pulse returns from the seabed 0.2 s after it was sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in the water. How deep is the water?

options.feedback: (1500 × 0.2) ÷ 2. The pulse covers the depth twice, so halve the total.
That is the total path of the pulse, down and back. The seabed is half as deep.
That halves twice. Halve the total distance once, and only once.
Speed divided by time is not a distance. Multiply the speed by the time, then halve.

items.stem: Why is the time halved in an echo calculation?

options.text: because the pulse travels to the reflector and back, covering twice the distance
options.feedback: That is the whole reason, and it is what the scheme wants written down.

options.text: because the echo is only half as loud as the pulse that was sent out
options.feedback: Loudness does not come into it. The halving is about the distance the pulse covered.

options.text: because sound travels more slowly on the way back
options.feedback: The speed is the same in both directions. What is doubled is the distance, not the time each metre takes.

items.stem: A student writes that ultrasound is part of the electromagnetic spectrum. What has gone wrong?

options.text: ultrasound is sound, so it is longitudinal and needs a medium; the electromagnetic one is ultraviolet
options.feedback: The two words look alike and mean quite different things. Examiners have seen ultrasound written where ultraviolet was wanted.

options.text: nothing: ultrasound and ultraviolet are two names for the same wave
options.feedback: They are different families. Ultrasound is a sound wave; ultraviolet is an electromagnetic wave.

options.text: ultrasound is electromagnetic, but it sits outside the seven named regions
options.feedback: Ultrasound is not electromagnetic at all. It is sound above the range of human hearing.

items.stem: A clap is echoed back from a wall 85 m away after 0.5 s. What is the speed of sound?

options.feedback: The sound covered 2 × 85 m in 0.5 s, so the speed is that distance divided by the time.
Only one leg of the journey was counted. Double the distance before dividing by the time.
Distance multiplied by time is not a speed. Speed = distance ÷ time.
That doubles the distance twice over. One doubling is enough: out and back.

items.stem: An ultrasound probe works at 40 kHz. What is this frequency in Hz?

options.feedback: Kilo means a thousand, so multiply by 1000 before substituting into any equation.
The prefix was dropped altogether. Summer 2025 examiners reported the kilo prefix causing trouble on an ultrasound question.
Kilo is a thousand, not a hundred.
That is a million, which is the mega prefix. Kilo is a thousand.

parts.stem: State what is meant by ultrasound.

accepted: sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz
sound of frequency greater than 20 000 Hz

scheme.for: sound with a frequency greater than 20 000 Hz
scheme.examinerNote: The number carries the mark; 'very high-pitched sound' on its own does not.

hints: The specification gives one exact number for this.
parts.workedSolution: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency greater than 20 000 Hz, which is above the range a human ear can hear.

commonErrors.feedback: Ultraviolet is electromagnetic, a kind of light; ultrasound is sound. The definition wanted is sound with a frequency greater than 20 000 Hz.

accepted: measuring the head diameter of a foetus
scanning a foetus in the womb

scheme.for: measuring foetal head diameter / scanning an unborn baby
scheme.examinerNote: The specification names the foetal head diameter; any scan of a foetus is credited.

hints: The specification names one medical use, and it involves a measurement.
parts.workedSolution: Ultrasound is used to measure the head diameter of a foetus during a pregnancy scan.

parts.stem: Give one use of ultrasound in industry.

accepted: finding cracks in a metal casting

parts.workedSolution: Ultrasound is used to detect defects inside metals: an echo comes back early from a crack, before the echo from the far face arrives.

context.setting: A walker shouting across a quarry and timing the echo

parts.stem:
A walker shouts towards a cliff face and hears the echo 0.8 s later. Sound travels through the air at 340 m/s.
Calculate the distance from the walker to the cliff.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

scheme.for: d = 272 m, the distance there and back
scheme.examinerNote: The total distance earns its mark before it is halved (the Summer 2019 Higher scheme); halving the time first reaches the same answer.

hints: The shout goes to the cliff and comes back, so the timed journey is twice the distance you want.
Work out the total distance first, then halve it.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t, so d = v × t = 340 × 0.8 = 272 m. That is the path to the cliff and back, so the cliff is 272 ÷ 2 = 136 m away.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the total distance the sound travelled, to the cliff and back. It keeps the equation, substitution and total-distance marks; the last mark needs it halved, because the cliff is one journey away.
The factor of two has been used twice: halve the total once, or halve the time once, never both.

context.setting: An air traffic radar tracking an aircraft over the Irish Sea

parts.stem:
A radar station sends a short pulse of radio waves towards an aircraft. The reflected pulse arrives back at the station 0.0004 s after it was sent. Radio waves travel at $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s.
Calculate the distance from the station to the aircraft.
Give your answer in km.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.
m → km is ÷ 1000; the question asks for kilometres.

hints: Radar uses electromagnetic waves, so the speed is the speed of light.
Work in metres first, then convert to kilometres at the end.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t, so d = v × t = 3 × 10⁸ × 0.0004 = 120 000 m: the path to the aircraft and back. The aircraft is half of that, 60 000 m away, and dividing by 1000 gives 60 km.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole journey of the pulse, out to the aircraft and back again. The aircraft is half as far away.
The halving is right but the answer is still in metres. The question asks for kilometres, so divide by 1000.

parts.stem:
An engineer places an ultrasound probe on a steel casting. An echo returns from a crack 0.0002 s after the pulse was sent. Ultrasound travels through this steel at 6000 m/s.
Calculate how far below the surface the crack lies.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: The pulse reaches the crack and comes back to the same probe.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t, so d = v × t = 6000 × 0.0002 = 1.2 m: down to the crack and back. The crack is half of that, 0.6 m, below the surface.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole path the pulse took, down to the crack and back to the probe. The equation and substitution stand; halve it for the depth.

context.setting: A class measuring the speed of sound by timing an echo from a sports hall wall

parts.stem:
A class stands 51 m from a flat sports hall wall. They clap once and hear the echo 0.3 s later.
Calculate the speed of sound in the air of the hall.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: The clap has to reach the wall and come back before anyone hears it.
The distance the sound covers is not 51 m.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t. The sound goes to the wall and back, so it covers 2 × 51 = 102 m in 0.3 s: v = 102 ÷ 0.3 = 340 m/s. Halving the time instead, 51 ÷ 0.15, gives the same.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one leg of the journey was used. The timed 0.3 s covers 51 m out and 51 m back, so double the distance before dividing. Summer 2024 examiners named this and its twin, forgetting to halve, in the same sentence.

context.setting: A harbour survey vessel and an airport control tower

parts.stem:
A survey vessel uses sonar to map the seabed.
Name the type of wave a sonar system sends out.

scheme.examinerNote: Sonar is sound under water; radar is the electromagnetic one.

hints: The clue is in the word: sonar is built on sound.
parts.workedSolution: Sonar sends out pulses of sound (usually ultrasound) and listens for the echo from the seabed or from objects under the water.

parts.stem: State the type of wave that radar uses to detect aircraft and ships.

scheme.examinerNote: The specification pairs sonar with sound pulses and radar with electromagnetic waves.

hints: Radar has to work through air over many kilometres, and very fast.
parts.workedSolution: Radar uses electromagnetic waves — radio waves or microwaves — which travel at the speed of light and reflect from aircraft and ships.

context.setting: An ultrasound cleaning bath in a jeweller's workshop

parts.stem:
An ultrasonic cleaning bath sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz through water. Sound travels through the water at 1500 m/s.
Calculate the ultrasound's wavelength in the water.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

scheme.for: substitution: 1500 = f × λ with the speed in place

scheme.examinerNote: The conversion from kHz has its own mark: kilo is a thousand.

hints: Kilo means a thousand, so the frequency has to be turned into hertz first.
Check the size of the answer: at 50 kHz in water a wavelength of a few centimetres is right, and a higher frequency would give a much shorter one.
parts.workedSolution: v = f λ, so λ = v ÷ f. The frequency must be in hertz: 50 kHz = 50 000 Hz. Then λ = 1500 ÷ 50 000 = 0.03 m.

commonErrors.feedback: The kilo was dropped: 50 kHz is 50 000 Hz, a thousand times more. The equation and the substitution stand; the conversion mark and the answer mark are lost. Summer 2025 Higher examiners reported the kilo prefix causing trouble in an ultrasound question like this one.

parts.stem:
A pulse is sent out and its echo returns after a time t. The wave travels at speed v.
Which expression gives the distance from the source to the reflector?

options.feedback: The pulse covers v × t altogether, and that is twice the distance you want.
That is the total path of the pulse, there and back. The reflector is half as far away.
Speed divided by time is not a distance. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
That doubles the total path instead of halving it, so the answer comes out four times too big.

hints: Ask what distance the timed journey actually covers.
parts.workedSolution: The pulse travels out to the reflector and back again, so in time t it covers v × t, which is twice the distance to the reflector. The distance is therefore (v × t) ÷ 2.

parts.stem: Explain why the calculation includes a division by two.

accepted: the pulse travels to the reflector and back, so it covers twice the distance

scheme.for: the pulse travels there and back / covers twice the distance in the measured time
scheme.examinerNote: The mark is for the there-and-back idea, not for the arithmetic.

hints: Think about what the stopwatch is actually timing.
parts.workedSolution: The stopwatch times the whole journey: out to the reflector and back again. That is twice the distance being asked for, so the total has to be halved.

commonErrors.feedback: The halving has nothing to do with how loud the echo is, or with the pulse slowing down; the speed is the same in both directions. It is there because the measured time covers two journeys, out and back.

parts.stem:
A fishing boat sends one sonar pulse straight down. The echo from the seabed arrives 0.1 s later. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water.
Calculate the depth of the water.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

scheme.for: d = 150 m, the distance there and back
scheme.examinerNote: The total distance earns its mark before it is halved (the Summer 2019 Higher scheme); halving the time first reaches the same answer.

hints: The pulse goes down to the seabed and back up to the boat.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t, so d = v × t = 1500 × 0.1 = 150 m: down to the seabed and back. The water is half of that, 75 m, deep.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole journey of the pulse, down and back. The equation, substitution and total stand; halve it for the depth.

parts.stem:
The same pulse also produced an earlier echo, arriving 0.04 s after the pulse was sent. This echo came from a shoal of fish.
Calculate the depth of the shoal.
hints: Same rule, different time.
An earlier echo must come from something closer.
parts.workedSolution: The same rule: 1500 × 0.04 = 60 m there and back, so the shoal is 60 ÷ 2 = 30 m down. Its echo arrived first because it is nearer the boat than the seabed.

commonErrors.feedback: The halving is missing again. Every echo distance is halved, because every echo is a there-and-back journey.

parts.stem: Use your answers to parts (a) and (b) to work out how far the shoal is above the seabed.
hints: Both depths are measured from the surface.
parts.workedSolution: Both depths are measured down from the surface, so the gap is 75 − 30 = 45 m.

context.setting: A sonographer measuring a foetal head from two echo times

figures.alt: A grey and black ultrasound scan of a foetus in the womb, with two electronic caliper crosses placed on the screen, one at each end of the body, and the measured length printed beside them.

figures.prompt: A real scan: here the calipers are measuring the baby's length, not the head diameter you are about to calculate. The machine works the same way for both. It prints a length from nothing but echo times, so which other quantity does it have to be told first?

parts.stem:
During a scan, an ultrasound pulse is sent into the mother. An echo from the near side of the baby's head returns 0.00008 s after the pulse was sent. Ultrasound travels through the tissue at 1500 m/s.
Calculate the depth of the near side of the head below the probe.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: The same halving rule applies inside the body.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t, so d = v × t = 1500 × 0.00008 = 0.12 m, into the body and back out. The near side of the head is half of that, 0.06 m, below the probe.

commonErrors.feedback: The pulse went in and came back out, so the timed distance is twice the depth. Halve it.

parts.stem:
A second echo, from the far side of the head, returns 0.0002 s after the pulse was sent.
Calculate the depth of the far side of the head below the probe.
hints: Same rule, longer time, greater depth.

commonErrors.feedback: The halving is missing. Every echo depth is half the total path of the pulse.

parts.stem:
Use your answers to parts (a) and (b) to calculate the diameter of the baby's head.
Give your answer in cm.

scheme.examinerNote: m → cm is × 100; the question asks for centimetres.

hints: The head sits between the two depths you have found.
Convert the metres into centimetres at the end.
parts.workedSolution: The head stretches from 0.06 m to 0.15 m below the probe, so its diameter is 0.15 − 0.06 = 0.09 m. In centimetres that is 0.09 × 100 = 9 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The subtraction is right but the answer is still in metres. Multiply by 100 for centimetres.

context.setting: A note for the crew of a survey vessel explaining how their depth sounder works

parts.stem:
A survey vessel finds the depth of the water using a sonar depth sounder.
Describe how the depth sounder measures the depth, and explain why the measured time has to be halved.
Your written communication is marked here as well: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the specification's own scientific terms.

hints: Tell the story in order: send, reflect, receive, time, calculate, halve.
The halving needs a reason, not just an instruction.
parts.workedSolution: The depth sounder sends a short pulse of sound downwards from the hull of the vessel. The pulse travels through the water, reflects from the seabed and returns as an echo, which a detector on the vessel picks up. An electronic timer measures the time between the pulse leaving and the echo arriving. The speed of sound in sea water is already known, so the total distance travelled by the pulse can be found from distance = speed × time. That total is the journey down to the seabed and back up again, which is twice the depth, so the depth of the water is half of it.

parts.stem:
A survey ship's sonar pulse returns from the seabed 0.05 s after it is sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water.
Calculate the depth of the water.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so a correct equation is recalled and written before any number goes in: v = d/t, d = v × t or the echo rule with its ÷ 2 all earn this mark; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

scheme.for: d = 75 m, the distance there and back
scheme.examinerNote: The total distance earns its mark before it is halved (the Summer 2019 Higher scheme); halving the time first reaches the same answer.

hints: The pulse goes down to the seabed and back up to the ship.
parts.workedSolution: v = d/t, so d = v × t = 1500 × 0.05 = 75 m, down and back. The depth is half of that: 37.5 m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the path down to the seabed and back up. The equation, substitution and total stand; halve it for the depth.

parts.stem:
The ship's radar sends out pulses of microwaves, one region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum that has the longest wavelength.

scheme.examinerNote: The name only: radio waves have the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency; gamma rays are at the other end.

hints: The spectrum runs from the longest waves to the shortest: radio waves first, gamma rays last.
parts.workedSolution: In order of decreasing wavelength the spectrum runs radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays, so the longest wavelength belongs to radio waves.

commonErrors.feedback: Gamma rays are the other end of the spectrum: the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency. The longest wavelength belongs to radio waves.

parts.stem:
The radar echo from a buoy returns 0.00002 s after the pulse is sent. Microwaves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Calculate the distance from the ship to the buoy.
hints: Radar is electromagnetic: the same echo rule, a much faster wave.
parts.workedSolution: d = v × t = 3 × 10⁸ × 0.00002 = 6000 m out and back, so the buoy is 3000 m away.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the pulse's path out to the buoy and back again. Halve it for the distance to the buoy.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dara is asked: 'A sonar pulse sent from a boat returns 0.16 s after it was sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. Calculate the depth of the water. [4]'
